title: Cybersecurity
examples: What is the difference between malware and a virus?
Can you give an example of a social engineering attack?
What is the best way to protect my personal data online?

explain.say: Today we are learning about keeping our digital information safe. Malware is any bad software designed to damage your computer. It can secretly steal your private information too.
Phishing is when attackers trick you into giving away passwords. They usually send fake emails that look very real to you. Always check the sender's actual email address first.
Social engineering uses human psychology to trick people. It does not involve technology at all. The attacker manipulates you into doing something unsafe.
Defences include using strong, unique passwords for every account. You should also enable two-factor authentication everywhere it is possible. This adds a vital second layer of security.
In real life, if you get a call from someone claiming to be from your bank. They might ask for your PIN number. You should hang up immediately and call the bank directly.
A common mistake is clicking links in emails without checking them first. Always hover your mouse over a link to see the real destination address. This simple check can prevent many problems.

faq.q: How does malware actually get onto my device?
faq.a: Malware often enters through infected downloads or by clicking bad links. You might also download something from a compromised website.
asks: What is the entry point for malware?

faq.q: Are there any signs that I have been phished?
faq.a: Signs include urgent requests for passwords or poor grammar in the email. The sender's address might look slightly wrong.
asks: How do I spot a fake email?
What should I look out for in emails?

faq.q: Is social engineering only done online?
faq.a: No, it can happen face to face in the real world. Someone might pretend to be a maintenance worker needing access.
asks: Where can I encounter social engineering?

faq.q: Is a strong password enough defence?
faq.a: No, a strong password is important but not enough on its own. You must also use two-factor authentication for better security.
asks: What is the best defence against hacking?
Do I need more than just a password?

faq.q: What is the difference between a virus and a worm?
faq.a: A virus needs a host program to spread, while a worm can spread independently across a network. Both are types of malware.
asks: What is the difference between malware types?
Do all malware need a file to run?

facts: Malware is a broad term covering many types of malicious software.
Phishing attacks often target credentials like usernames and passwords.
Social engineering exploits human trust rather than technical flaws.
Two-factor authentication requires a second verification method.

quiz.say: You receive an email from your 'bank' asking you to click a link to verify your account details immediately.
quiz.why: This is a classic example of phishing because it uses a fake message to trick you into giving up sensitive information.

wrong.0: Defence is the solution, not the threat being described in the scenario.
wrong.2: Malware is the bad software itself, not the trick used to get you to install it.
wrong.3: While phishing uses social engineering, the specific tactic of fake emails is best called phishing.

quiz.say: A stranger calls pretending to be from IT support and asks you to install remote access software on your computer.
quiz.why: The attacker is manipulating you by pretending to be someone trustworthy to gain unauthorized access.

wrong.0: Phishing usually involves electronic communication, like email or text messages.
wrong.1: Malware is the resulting bad software, not the act of the trick itself.
wrong.2: This describes the attack, not the protective measure you should take.

quiz.say: To protect your online accounts, you should use a mix of strong passwords and a second verification step.
quiz.why: Using two-factor authentication adds a crucial second layer of defence beyond just a password.

wrong.0: While caution is needed, sometimes links are legitimate, so total avoidance is not practical.
wrong.1: Updating software patches technical holes, but it does not stop human trickery.
wrong.3: Strong passwords are necessary, but they can sometimes be guessed or cracked over time.
